extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, judges, and law students studying patent amendment/disclaimer law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing the use of disclaimers to amend excessive or defective patent claims: when a disclaimer is permitted, who may file it, how it must be made, its legal effect, and timing consequences (including effect on costs and suits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer allowed only for inadvertent errors (no fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive Claim can be amended by disclaimer only when the error arose through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law requires utmost good faith; a patentee who wilfully misleads the public cannot use a disclaimer to cure errors. Case citations and commentary emphasize that disclaimers are denied where the defect grew out of wilful deception (see Schillinger v. Gunther and related authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amended claim must cover a patentable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim can be amended by disclaimer only when the Claim as amended would cover a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee cannot retain rights to anything not lawfully patentable; the portion retained after disclaimer must be material, substantial, separable, and itself patentable. If the part rightfully claimed is not distinguishable or is not a patentable invention, disclaimer is improper (Hotchkiss v. Oliver examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer not permitted after unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive Claim can be amended by disclaimer only when the amendment is attempted without unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay equates to forfeiting the privilege to amend and is a question for the court based on facts. Delay begins when the patentee becomes aware that he has claimed more than invented or described. Allowance of claims by the Patent Office may create a presumption favoring the patentee until a court decides otherwise. A disclaimer cannot be filed after the patent has expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a disclaimer (ownership/interest limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer must be filed by a party owning an interest in the patent and whose interest is distinct from that of co-owners; an owner of the entire patent or of an entire territorial interest may file; an original patentee cannot disclaim after parting with entire title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An owner of an undivided interest cannot unilaterally disclaim without cooperation of other co-owners; a territorial disclaimant limits the patent only as to his interest and those deriving title after the disclaimer. An attorney's disclaimer does not necessarily bind the patentee. Under some English authorities a patentee who has parted with his interest could file, but U.S. practice requires ownership of the interest being disclaimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content requirements for a disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer must be in writing, signed by the disclaimant, attested by one or more witnesses, recorded in the Patent Office, state the exact interest of the disclaimant, and distinctly set out the excess to be disclaimed, averring it was included through inadvertence, accident, or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclaimer fails to state the disclaimant's interest it can be invalid. Upon recording, the disclaimer is considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest and those who take title after recording. A disclaimer may relate to figures in drawings and may remove descriptive matter that solely supported the disclaimed excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer not a method to amend defective description
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer cannot be employed to alter or reform the Description; it only eliminates superfluous matter from the Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Description requires amendment to give effect to a Claim, or a Claim demands restatement to avoid obscurity, or new Claims are necessary, these must be sought by re-issue, not by disclaimer. Although descriptive matter incidental to a disclaimed excess may be withdrawn, a disclaimer cannot change the character of the invention or create a new patentable scope (Haileas v. Albany Stove Co., Union Metallic Cartridge Co. v. United States Cartridge Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer's effect limited to removed excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a disclaimer is confined to the excess which it removes from the apparent protection of the patent; otherwise the patent remains operative as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer does not add to the patent nor broaden protection. It does not affect other valid claims standing by themselves. Disclaiming a species does not necessarily affect a genus claim; disclaimed matter is treated as if never part of the patent for construction purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent read as amended; interpretation without disclaimed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: After disclaimer the patent stands read as if the disclaimer were incorporated into the original specification; both Claims and Descriptions are interpreted without reference to withdrawn matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclaimer is considered part of the specification upon recording. Objectionable phrases may be removed provided no new construction is given to remaining text. A disclaimer cannot be used to make remaining parts retroactively valid if they were unsupported (cases: Dunbar v. Myers; Schillinger v. Cranford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of disclaimer relative to litigation affects costs and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a disclaimer before the commencement of suit (and with reasonable diligence) preserves the patentee's entitlement to costs; filing after suit generally allows recovery on valid claims but typically without costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the acts discussed (1836/1837 and later), a plaintiff who files a proper disclaimer prior to suit may recover costs; if filed during or after suit the plaintiff may still recover damages for the valid invention but will not be entitled to costs unless no unreasonable delay occurred. Courts have discretion on costs where defendants have used any part of the truly claimed invention. The treatise discusses section 7/9 provisos and many cases (Guyon v. Serrell; Hall v. Wiles; Tuck v. Bramhill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer is nullity if no real excess exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer filed without sufficient cause is a nullity; if the original Claim was not actually excessive, filing a disclaimer does not admit inability to recover costs and is inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer that leaves the patent claiming the entire invention as courts would construe it is ineffective both as an amendment and for cost consequences. Similarly, disclaimers of parts not actually claimed are inoperative. The burden lies on those alleging original fraud to prove it when contesting a disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers cannot be used to obtain rights to un-described matter or create new patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer cannot be used to make a patent cover what is not described or claimed as part of the invention or to convert a Claim into one for something else; it cannot produce new patentable scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee seeks to change the character of the invention or to obtain coverage for matter not described, the proper remedy is surrender and re-issue (or obtaining a new patent), not a disclaimer. Disclaimers are solely to eliminate separable excess; any attempt to use them to expand rights is rejected by courts (White v. Gleason Mfg. Co.; Foxwell v. Bostock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectional/territorial disclaimers and their local effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer filed by a sectional or territorial owner limits the patent only as to the interest owned by that disclaimant; the same patent may be operative to different extents in different territories or as to different owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After such disclaimer, the patent in effect makes distinct claims of right in different sections of the country, potentially resulting in 'two specifications' for the same invention: one operative for the disclaimant's section and another for others. The patent as amended will limit and define the disclaimant's rights while other parties hold under the patent in its original form.

rubrics_metrics.name: When disclaimer withdraws re-issue/new matter, remaining new matter may be discarded
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a disclaimer withdraws a new re-issue claim and leaves only what was covered by the original, any new matter remaining in the Description must be discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer that effectively nullifies the new re-issue Claim cannot leave stray new matter in the specification; courts have required that such new matter be discarded if not properly supported by the original (Schillinger v. Cranford and related authority).
